meta.date: ~600 BC (before the departure from the valley)

world_behind.title: A family they already knew
world_behind.text: The sons go straight to "the house of Ishmael" (v. 4), gain a hearing, and persuade an entire household to abandon Jerusalem, a result that makes best sense if the families were already connected, perhaps by long acquaintance or existing marriage expectations. The record spends one verse on what was likely a far longer negotiation.

world_behind.title: Jeremiah in prison dates the chapter
world_behind.text: Nephi's evidence that the city's probation is closing is current news: "Jeremiah have they cast into prison" (v. 14). Jeremiah's imprisonments under Zedekiah are documented in his own book (Jer. 37–38), and the detail pins the record's chronology to checkable public history.

spans.text: Jeremiah have they cast into prison

world_behind.title: What the rebels were giving up, again
world_behind.text: For Ishmael's older children the journey meant walking away from property, betrothal prospects, and standing. It was the same loss Laman counted in chapter 2. The desire to "return unto the land of Jerusalem" (v. 7) was not perversity; it was ordinary practical sense, aimed at a city with a decade to live.

cites.quote: return unto the land of Jerusalem

spans.text: return unto the land of Jerusalem

world_behind.title: Abandonment as execution
world_behind.text: Binding a man and leaving him "to be devoured by wild beasts" (v. 16) was murder with no blood on anyone's hands and no body to answer for. The plan's cold practicality, an untraceable death in empty country, is part of the record's honesty about how far the family's division had gone.

world_behind.title: Five daughters, three sons, and a colony's future
world_behind.text: The Lord's instruction that the sons "should take daughters to wife, that they might raise up seed unto the Lord" (v. 1) frames marriage as covenant business: a promised land is no inheritance without heirs. Jeremiah wrote the same instruction to the exiles in Babylon that same generation: take wives, bear children, be increased (Jer. 29:6).

world_behind.title: The flood formula
world_behind.text: "The Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them" (v. 14) quotes the sentence spoken over the generation of Noah (Gen. 6:3). Hearers raised on the brass plates would catch the echo: Jerusalem is being cast as the doomed world, and the family as the remnant already aboard.

spans.text: The Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them

words.text: "It was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone" (v. 1) means fit, suitable, proper. The word carries heaven's assessment of a solitary colonization: not wrong but unfit, a plan that cannot carry the promise it exists for. The correction is practical before it is doctrinal, and the errand it launches supplies the colony's future.

cites.quote: It was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone

words.text: "We did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael" (v. 4): a diplomacy word. After chapters of lots, gold, and a sword, the second Jerusalem errand runs entirely on goodwill and softened hearts. The contrast is the point: what the record's God does to Laban and what he does to Ishmael are both called deliverance, and only one required a blade.

words.text: Before the rebuke, the record names the feeling behind it: "being grieved for the hardness of their hearts" (v. 8). Grief, not anger, and the reader is told so before the hard questions begin. It is the same word for the same cause as in the valley, where his brothers' hardness sent him to his knees rather than to a speech (1 Ne. 2:18).

words.text: "If it so be that they exercise faith in him" (v. 12): faith as something a person puts to work. The verb enters the record here and the record keeps it. Alma will build an entire sermon on the same picture, beginning with a particle of faith exercised (Alma 32:27). Between the two passages the meaning does not move: faith is measured by use.

cites.quote: If it so be that they exercise faith in him

spans.text: If it so be that they exercise faith in him

words.text: "If ye have choice, go up to the land" (v. 15). Choice here is a noun for preference, the thing a man would rather do, and Nephi hands it to men who have just heard what going will cost them. Everywhere else this record says choice it is an adjective for excellence: a land choice above all other lands (1 Ne. 2:20), a choice seer, choice men. The one place the word names a human power, it is being offered to rebels.

cites.quote: If ye have choice, go up to the land

spans.text: If ye have choice, go up to the land

words.text: Nephi prays for strength to burst his bands; instead "the bands were loosed from off my hands and feet" (v. 18). The record's first bonds-and-deliverance miracle sets a pattern the volume will repeat in prisons and camps for centuries, and it starts with the detail that God answered the need.

phrases.term: Raise up seed unto the Lord
phrases.text: The errand's purpose clause. Seed raised unto the Lord is lineage framed as offering. The children are the covenant's future membership. The phrase quietly recasts the whole marriage journey: Ishmael's daughters are being recruited to a promise.

phrases.term: How is it that ye have forgotten
phrases.text: Three times in three verses: the angel (v. 10), the deliverance from Laban (v. 11), the Lord's power (v. 12). Nephi's rebuke is structured as a memory examination, and the diagnosis matches the record's standing theory of unbelief: his brothers have seen everything and retained nothing. Rebellion, in this family, is a failure of remembering before it is a failure of nerve.

phrases.term: The Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive
phrases.text: Striving is sustained contention, patience applied against resistance over time. Here it comes with a deadline. The sentence is the record's most sobering borrowing: Noah's generation heard it first (Gen. 6:3), and Nephi's descendants will hear it again as doctrine (2 Ne. 26:11). Applied to Jerusalem it means the city's probation has a closing time, and the imprisoned Jeremiah (v. 14) is the visible countdown.

phrases.term: According to my faith which is in thee
phrases.text: The prayer indexes its request to faith, not to desert: deliver me according to what I actually trust thee for. It is a measurable prayer, and the answer measures back generously, loosing what Nephi asked for strength to burst. The exchange teaches how this record prays: name the faith you have, and let God choose the mechanism.

Frankly meant freely (whole, open, nothing reserved for later), and the adverb carries the scene's ethics: pardon given entire, the same day the cords came off. It is the rebellion cycle's closing step: sorrow (v. 20), frank forgiveness, then "I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness" (v. 21). Nephi forgives fully and immediately, and then declines to be the final court, sending the offense where it actually lies.

cites.quote: I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness

spans.text: I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A journey sent back for a stated demographic reason
verses.text: The record gives the instruction and the reasoning behind it in one sentence: "it was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone; but that his sons should take daughters to wife, that they might raise up seed unto the Lord in the land of promise." The problem is the survival of a population, and the remedy is a second expedition to the city they have just left. Nothing in the verse is framed as a test or a trial.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: The persuasion reported and not given
verses.text: The record says that words were spoken and declines to supply them: "we did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael, insomuch that we did speak unto him the words of the Lord." What is reported instead is the outcome and its cause, "the Lord did soften the heart of Ishmael, and also his household, insomuch that they took their journey with us down into the wilderness to the tent of our father." A whole family's decision to abandon a city is covered in two clauses, one of which is about God rather than about argument.

verses.label: v. 6
verses.title: A rebellion counted by household, and one family splits
verses.text: The record names the parties rather than describing the mood: "Laman and Lemuel, and two of the daughters of Ishmael, and the two sons of Ishmael and their families, did rebel against us." Ishmael's household is divided down the middle in the same sentence that reports the rebellion, since two daughters and two sons go one way and the rest do not. The precision is unusual, and it makes the party's later composition legible.

verses.label: v. 9–12
verses.title: Four questions, three of them about forgetting
verses.text: The reply to the rebellion is entirely interrogative and each verse opens the same way: "How is it that ye have not hearkened unto the word of the Lord?", "How is it that ye have forgotten that ye have seen an angel of the Lord?", "how is it that ye have forgotten what great things the Lord hath done for us, in delivering us out of the hands of Laban?", "how is it that ye have forgotten that the Lord is able to do all things?" One asks about obedience and three about memory, and the record answers none of them.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: A date fixed against a book the reader already has
verses.text: The argument for not returning is anchored to an event outside the volume: "they have rejected the prophets, and Jeremiah have they cast into prison." Jer. 37:15 reports the imprisonment, so the record is placing its own narrative inside a chronology its readers can check elsewhere. The same verse gives the reason the city cannot be safe, "the Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them."

chapter.title: The unit's mirror journey
chapter.text: The second return replays the first with the hardware swapped out: no lots, no gold, no sword; favor and softening instead. Read as a pair, chapters 3–4 and 7 teach that the Lord's errands do not have a fixed method; they have a fixed completion.

chapter.title: Chapter 2's diagnosis, demonstrated
chapter.text: The record said early that the brothers "knew not the dealings of that God who had created them" (1 Ne. 2:12); this chapter stages the proof. An angel has stood in front of these men, and it changed nothing that lasted. Between the two chapters the record completes a claim it will hold for a thousand years: seeing is not keeping.

chapter.title: The violence comes home
chapter.text: Chapter 3's rod becomes cords and a planned death by exposure. The record does not soften its founding family: the future division of nations begins as attempted fratricide, twice restrained: once by an angel, this time by women pleading.

chapter.title: Ishmael's unremarked faith
chapter.text: The chapter's greatest believer gets no speech: an established householder who hears "the words of the Lord" (v. 4) and moves his entire family into a wilderness. The record says almost nothing about him, and the silence is its own comment. Some obedience is so complete it leaves nothing to narrate.

chapter.title: Reconciliation follows a sequence
chapter.text: Plea, softening, sorrow, bowing, pardon, prayer (v. 19–21): the record's first full forgiveness scene runs every step in order and ends at an altar (v. 22). The sequence, not just the sentiment, is what the chapter preserves, and later reruns of family rebellion will be measured against it.

chapter.title: The departures unit closes at the altar
chapter.text: Sacrifice and burnt offerings (v. 22) bookend the unit with chapter 5's homecoming worship: two returns, two altars. The colony now holds its scripture, its families, and a working pattern for surviving its own worst members. The vision cycle of chapters 8–15 will test all three.

applications.title: Keep an angel ledger
applications.text: The brothers' collapse was a failure to hold on to what they had already seen. Keep a running list of the three or four unmistakable interventions in your life, and read it whenever a hard assignment makes them convenient to forget.

applications.title: Pray the faith you have
applications.text: In your next urgent prayer, say out loud what you actually trust God for in this specific matter (no more, no less), then ask from there. Honesty about the size of your faith is not weakness in prayer; in this chapter it is the thing heaven answers.

applications.title: Be the pleader
applications.text: The scene was turned by people who took no side but peace. In the next locked conflict near you (family, ward, workplace) try the daughter-of-Ishmael role: plead with the angry on behalf of the endangered, and let softened hearts do what argument could not.

applications.title: Forgive frankly, then route it upward
applications.text: Installment forgiveness keeps the debt alive. Practice the chapter's form: full pardon stated plainly to the person, and the offense referred to God, the same day if it can be managed.

applications.title: Speak from the station you hold
applications.text: Nephi's authority in the scene was nothing but clarity and example: a younger brother with neither rank nor leverage. Where you are junior and the truth is being forgotten, say it anyway, and let the example carry what the seniority cannot.

applications.title: End reconciliations at an altar
applications.text: The family's quarrel does not end with the apology; it ends with shared worship. Close your next repaired relationship the same way, with a prayer together, a meal blessed, or a sabbath kept jointly, so the peace has somewhere to live.

questions.text: Whose heart am I still trying to argue open that only softening, and my own patience, could actually reach?
Which Jerusalem keeps pulling me back: the comfortable thing I know is scheduled for demolition, but is still home?
What have I personally seen of God that I have functionally forgotten, and where is it written down, if anywhere?
Where do I owe someone a plain statement of consequences and a genuinely free choice, instead of pressure?
In the conflicts around me, am I a combatant, a spectator, or a pleader, and which does my family need this month?
Is there a forgiveness I have granted only in installments, and what would granting it frankly cost me?
